The airport comes to you.

Floating Skyports

No runways. No terminals. No fixed infrastructure. Just an airborne pickup point that moves to where the demand is.

01

The idea

Unbolt the airport from the ground.

Airports are ground infrastructure: runways, terminals, gates, all fixed in place. What if the airport floats, moves, and comes to you?

The first version is deliberately simple. Put the load on a platform. Push up from below. Keep every lifting vessel in direct physical contact with the deck, held snug by a net hanging from the platform. The platform does not need to fly by itself. The lifters carry it.

02

The system

A pickup location in the sky.

Massive lifting vessels — airships today, HEAR-TS at scale — press against the underside of a working platform. Nets hang from the deck and hold the lifters tight to it. The contact is structural: lift goes straight into the platform.

The platform is not a city and it is not a terminal. It is a pickup location. Small VTOL craft dock with it, transfer people or cargo, then leave: air taxis, delivery drones, light cargo hoppers. Hub and spoke, all airborne.

Lift

Large vessels carry the deck and its long-haul load.

Dock

Small VTOL craft meet the platform without a runway.

Move

The whole pickup point repositions with demand.

03

Modular lift

Build lift like a fleet, not a monument.

Tether the lifters together under one platform. Add ships when the load grows. Pull ships away when it shrinks.

More ships means more lift. Fewer ships means less. The fleet can add vertical capacity, reposition power where the platform needs it, or change the makeup of the cluster without replacing the whole structure.

MORE LIFTERS→MORE PLATFORM→MORE LOAD

Think twenty strung together, lifting a whole factory. The answer to needing a bigger airship does not have to be one impossible envelope. It can be a coordinated swarm carrying one shared deck.

04

The lanes

Three jobs. One moving hub.

Delivery

Packages ride up once. Drones fan out for the last mile.

Taxi

Air taxis move people between local pickup points and the long-haul platform.

Light cargo

Fast hoppers connect factories, ships, settlements, and cities.

05

The fleets

Twenty-four fleets. One moving clock.

One fleet per timezone, rotating around Earth. Each aims to reach the next timezone before the sun does — or just in time.

The airport is no longer a place you travel to. It is a machine that travels with you.

Now you sit at the airport for 3 hours going nowhere. Later you sit at the airport for 3 hours with “connecting” flights to airports going other ways — and are closer.

There are no fixed tracks and no mandatory direction around the planet. Fleets go all which ways, following where the airplanes, passengers, and cargo need to go. Demand sets the route.

06

The trick

Let each machine do what it is good at.

The big lifters do the long, slow, efficient haul. The little craft do the short, fast legs.

Do not make a delivery drone cross a continent. Do not make an enormous lifting vessel land for every package. The skyport is the interchange: one heavy airborne backbone, many quick local branches.

07

The fuel

A hydrogen pipeline in the sky.

The fleet uses hydrogen as lifting gas and burns it for propulsion. Docked VTOLs refuel at the platform. Surplus feeds into the D-Mom ocean hydrogen network.

The same moving infrastructure carries freight, energy, and the fuel for its own local fleet.

“Where we're going, we don't need roads.”

Doc Brown · Back to the Future

The punchline

No ground airports.

No runways. No terminals. No fixed anything. The pickup point drifts to demand.

Scratched
(for now)

Lifting a Starship with airships. It needs roughly 20× the lift and 3× the altitude of anything flying. Shelved until the lifters get bigger. The skyport survives because it does not carry the rocket — it carries the interchange.

The airport is no longer a place you travel to. It is a machine that travels to you.
